paragraphs.source_en: The hypothesis of a fusion of Central Saharan hunters with the herders is plausible especially in the later phases of the Pastoral period. The documentation from the Acacus (Barich 2002) dates the late Pastoral Neolithic to between 5,000 and 3,800 BP. In this phase, except for small, probably transitory, camps and hearth places, the lowlands were progressively abandoned because of the increasing aridity and life became concentrated in the mountains. Hunters and pastoralists must have shared a restricted territory and this was likely to have had a definitive impact on the disintegration of most of the hunting society and on the changing process in the adopted subsistence strategies.

paragraphs.source_en: Another hypothesis regarding the final stages of the Round Head art is that some hunter-gatherer groups abandoned the Central Sahara in the arid period. What was the most probable route of the migration? Considering the geographical conditions, they were unlikely to migrate northwards as the large plains were too arid to cross. A more suitable way to migrate was to the south. Not only were the main rivers flowing to the south but also there are hills and mountains until the Chad basin. People could have followed these mountains where the aridity was certainly less marked, or they could have followed the wadies which probably still had some water even during increasing aridity.

paragraphs.source_en: The hypothesis for the migration of people to the south is supported by the fact that wild fauna also migrated spontaneously in the same direction, namely from the Central Saharan massifs towards the Chad basin and the river Niger (Maley 2004). The southward retreat of the tsetse-fly belts resulted in a general southerly movement, particularly along watercourses running north/south from the Sahara (Williams 1984). Lake Chad or the Niger Delta would have proved an attractive magnet to peoples fleeing the final desiccation of the Sahara. Indeed, the earliest pottery at Jenne-jeno in southern Mali dating at 250 B. C. shows unmistakable Saharan affinities (McIntosh 1983; McIntosh Keech 1995). It is also in the sub-Saharan Africa where we find impressive affinities between the still used masks and those represented in the Round Head art.
